Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty Images Andy Burnham Analysis Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral asset Kiran Stacey Policy editor While a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overall UK politics live – latest updates Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.18 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.32 EDT Share There was a time when placing Israel under strict trade sanctions would have been a politically risky thing for a British prime minister to do. Andy Burnham , however, considers it an electoral asset. As Kemi Badenoch attacked him over defence spending at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham deliberately turned the topic to the trade ban on illegal settlements which he had announced on Tuesday. With the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, sitting to his left, the prime minister said: “In this difficult and dangerous world Britain has to stand for something, Britain has to show leadership, Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice. “Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them. That, Mr Speaker, is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about. “That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.” Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk Read more Under the new sanctions announced on Tuesday , goods produced in illegal settlements in occupied Palestine will be banned from being imported into the UK and those who help build or finance settlements will face sanctions. The measures drew a sharp response from the Israeli government, which announced the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Domestically, the opposition has been led by Badenoch, who has long been a staunch ally of Israel. In a piece in the Jewish Chronicle , the Conservative leader warned that the prime minister risked “fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home”. “For all Labour claim to have rooted out antisemitism internally, the degree of anti-Israel hatred means that Labour’s approach to many of these issues is Corbyn in all but name,” she added. Others in her party, however, have struck a less aggressive tone. On Tuesday, the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said: “None of us here rejects the government’s stated aim that we must do everything we can to end the circle of violence and support the Abraham accords and the two-state solution. “What we reject is performative politics, acting alone, that leaves our envoys irrelevant and our voice weaker.” Some senior Conservatives even backed the government. Edward Leigh, who as father of the house has held his seat longer than any other MP, told the Commons on Tuesday: “I am proud to say that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today, because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and for justice for all people in this world.” I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy Burnham Read more The government has reason to believe it is on strong electoral ground with this decision. A poll by YouGov earlier in the summer found 50% of British voters supported a ban on trade with West Bank settlements, while only 16% were opposed. While Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters were the strongest backers of such a move, even Conservative and Reform voters were in favour overall. Labour officials hope the announcement may help them make up ground with progressive and Muslim voters who have moved away from the party since the 2024 election. Many say they remain angry about an interview given by Keir Starmer soon after the Gaza war began in which the then prime minister said he thought Israel had the right to withhold water and electricity from Palestinians. The disillusionment among Muslim voters was particularly important in the Green party’s victory in Gorton and Denton . Meanwhile Labour lost a large part of its broader progressive base during the local elections, in which the Greens took a number of councils and mayoralties in central London. Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, tweeted on Tuesday : “Ed Miliband’s statement on Israel is only a first step. We need to go further: a full ban on goods, services & investment.” Labour and the Greens are now again locked in battle, over the Holborn and St Pancras seat, which Starmer has vacated . Though the policy was in train long before that byelection was called, it could prove an important campaign tool for Labour canvassers looking to reassure their core voters. Morgan and another prestigious US financial firm The Finance Minister will hold a series of economic and financial meetings aimed at attracting US capital for strategic projects and strengthening dialogue with international investors. These meetings will involve representatives from prestigious US banks and financial institutions—such as J.P. Morgan and Exim Bank, among others—according to a statement released by the Ministry of Finance on Monday. On Monday, Alexandru Nazare will participate in a roundtable titled „Anchoring the Eastern Flank: Critical Infrastructure and Transatlantic Capital in Central and Eastern Europe,” organized by the Atlantic Council Romania in New York. The event brings together US institutional investors, development finance institutions, representatives of transatlantic policy organizations, and government and diplomatic officials from the region. Also on Monday, the Finance Minister will meet with representatives from J.P. Morgan and institutional investors with exposure to Romanian government securities. Discussions will focus on public finance trends, continued fiscal consolidation, the state’s financing strategy, and Romania’s economic outlook. Regarding the prior dialogue with representatives of J.P. During the most recent meeting held in Bucharest, discussions focused on the deficit trajectory, financing costs, the continuation of reforms, and the absorption of European funds—given that fiscal predictability and credibility directly influence the terms under which Romania secures financing on international markets, according to the cited source. On Tuesday, Alexandru Nazare will meet with Ben Black, CEO of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC)—the U.S. government agency that mobilizes private capital and finances investments in strategic sectors such as infrastructure, energy, and advanced technology. Further discussions will take place in Bucharest regarding potential financing instruments for Romanian strategic projects and attracting American capital into the economy. Over the past year, Romania has engaged in discussions with the DFC, the U.S. EXIM Bank, and U.S. Congressional representatives to strengthen the economic pillar of the Strategic Partnership with the United States. These talks covered energy, infrastructure, and production capacity, as well as the integration of Romanian companies into transatlantic supply chains. „The New York visit program continues Minister Alexandru Nazare’s efforts to strengthen the economic component of the relationship with the United States and to ensure a more active presence for Romania within major international capital and investment flows,” the Ministry of Finance concluded.
